Container.Name: github-runner
Container.Overview: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner, one instance per repository. On a PRIVATE repository its minutes do not count against the account's Actions allowance, which is the usual reason to run one (GitHub-hosted runners are already free for public repositories). Nothing in this template names a repository or a host: set ACCESS_TOKEN, REPO_URL, RUNNER_NAME and LABELS per instance and the runner registers itself on start, appearing under the repository's Settings -> Actions -> Runners. With a single runner, a workflow selects it with runs-on: self-hosted. TWO WARNINGS, both expanded in the field descriptions below. First, the Docker socket mount makes a workflow effectively root on this host, and nothing here is a containment boundary: run only repositories whose workflow code you control, and never one where a fork pull request can run attacker-authored code. Second, RUNNER_NAME and LABELS appear in the job log of every run, world-readable on a public repository, so neither should name the machine. Network mode host is deliberate and is explained on the Docker socket field. One runner runs ONE job at a time; for concurrency add another instance with its own container Name, RUNNER_NAME and distinguishing label.
Container.Description: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner (neutral template, one instance per repository). Set the PAT, repository URL, runner name and labels at creation. Network mode host is deliberate. The image tag is pinned; the runner binary self-updates regardless of it.

Config.Name: Docker socket
Config.Description: Needed by any workflow that builds an image, declares a services: container, or uses an action that shells out to docker (build-push-action, buildx, testcontainers). WHY NETWORK MODE IS host: the runner asks the HOST's daemon for those containers, so a service container's published port lands in the HOST's network namespace. A bridge-mode container has its own namespace, so its localhost is not the host's and a workflow written the GitHub-hosted way cannot find its service there even though the service is up and healthy (it is still reachable via the docker bridge gateway, but only after a workflow change). host mode shares the host's namespace, so localhost means what it means on a GitHub-hosted runner. The cost is that the container then has no namespace of its own: a job can bind host ports and can reach services listening only on the host's 127.0.0.1, which a bridge container genuinely cannot. NOTE that a service is published to a host port only if the workflow asks — a bare `ports: - 5432` takes a RANDOM host port (read it from job.services.<id>.ports) and a fixed localhost:5432 needs `ports: - 5432:5432`; a fixed mapping occupies that host port for the life of the job in ANY network mode, so two runners running such a job at once collide. SECURITY: this mount grants control of the host's Docker daemon, which is equivalent to root on the host. If no workflow on this repository needs Docker, CLEAR THIS FIELD — a runner without the socket is dramatically less dangerous and it is the single biggest risk reduction available here.

Config.Name: ACCESS_TOKEN
Config.Description: GitHub Personal Access Token used to mint short-lived runner registration tokens. Fine-grained, scoped to this ONE repository, with Administration: read and write (the permission that mints a registration token) — not a classic token with blanket repo scope. It is used at START to register and again at STOP to deregister, so rotating it while a container is running leaves that runner unable to deregister and a stale offline entry on the repository's runner page; rotate and restart while the old token still works. With EPHEMERAL each job is a whole container lifecycle, so the token is used once per job. TREAT IT AS EXPOSED TO YOUR WORKFLOWS: Mask hides it in this UI only, and Unraid stores it in plain text in the container's template on the flash drive. The image un-exports it before starting the runner, so it is NOT in a step's own environment — but job steps run as root inside this container and can read it from /proc/1/environ, and with the Docker socket mounted a job can also read it from docker inspect of this very container. A compromised workflow is a compromised PAT.

Config.Name: REPO_URL
Config.Description: Full URL of the repository this runner serves: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> . No .git suffix and no trailing path — the owner and repository are cut straight out of this string, so a stray suffix produces a 404 when the registration token is requested and then an opaque config failure. This template is repository-scoped, so this is always a repository URL.

Config.Name: RUNNER_NAME
Config.Description: The name this runner registers under, e.g. <repo>-runner-1. It appears in the repository's runner list AND in the job log of every workflow run, which is world-readable on a public repository — so pick a name that reveals nothing about the machine. Must be unique: the runner registers with --replace, so a second instance sharing a name does NOT error, it silently takes over the first one's registration and the two then fight over one identity.

Config.Name: LABELS
Config.Description: Comma-separated labels a workflow selects this runner by. The runner also adds self-hosted, Linux and X64 itself (unless registered with NO_DEFAULT_LABELS, which this template does not expose), and once registered those cannot be deleted from its page. So the shipped value adds nothing on its own, and that is fine while this is your ONLY runner: runs-on: self-hosted already reaches it. BEFORE ADDING A SECOND RUNNER, give each a distinguishing label — e.g. self-hosted,<repo> — and target runs-on: [self-hosted, <that label>], or a job will pick whichever runner is free. Labels are public in workflow logs, so keep them neutral.

Config.Name: RUNNER_SCOPE
Config.Description: Leave at repo; it is here for completeness, not as a choice. The image also accepts org and ent, but those modes ignore REPO_URL and read ORG_NAME / ENTERPRISE_NAME instead, and this template exposes neither. If you set one anyway, the image DOES print a clear line naming the missing variable (ORG_NAME required for org runners) — but that check cannot stop the container, so it continues and fails a second time, opaquely, in config.sh. Read the FIRST message, not the last. An org-wide runner also accepts jobs from every repository in the org, so it is only as trustworthy as the least trustworthy workflow there.

Config.Name: RUNNER_WORKDIR
Config.Description: Where the runner checks code out INSIDE this container. Leave as-is for normal use — it is internal to the container and needs no host storage. Change it ONLY together with the optional work directory below, where the two must agree.

Config.Name: Work directory (optional)
Config.Description: OPTIONAL, normally left EMPTY. Needed when the host's daemon must bind-mount the workspace: a job running in a job container (the workflow container: key), a step using a Docker container action, or a service container that mounts the workspace. The runner asks the daemon to mount its OWN workspace path, so that path must resolve to the same data on the host — EDIT BOTH FIELDS so Container Path and Host Path are the IDENTICAL string, and set RUNNER_WORKDIR above to that string plus /work. Because they must match and Unraid's /tmp is RAM-backed, the container path has to move off /tmp too; that is why the shipped Container Path is not /tmp/runner. Example trio: container /mnt/POOL/appdata/gh-runner-1, host /mnt/POOL/appdata/gh-runner-1, RUNNER_WORKDIR /mnt/POOL/appdata/gh-runner-1/work — substituting your own pool. RUNNERS ON ONE HOST MUST NEVER SHARE THESE: give a second runner its own -2 set, or concurrent jobs corrupt each other's checkouts. Two consequences worth knowing: a path mismatch raises no clear error, surfacing instead as file-not-found failures inside the job container; and because sync-templates.py identifies a path mapping by its container path, changing it makes that script report your mapping as KEPT on later runs — expected here, not a template bug.

Config.Name: EPHEMERAL
Config.Description: OPTIONAL. Accepts exactly ONE job and then deregisters. ANY NON-EMPTY VALUE ENABLES IT, including the literal string false — to disable it, leave the field EMPTY. It also needs the container to come back afterwards, which neither this template nor Unraid configures: add --restart=unless-stopped under Extra Parameters (switch the page to Advanced View), or the runner simply disappears after its first job. What does NOT carry over is the registration. What DOES: this container's filesystem when the same container restarts, any mounted work directory, and every image, volume and build-cache entry the job left on the host daemon. It is not a containment boundary — with the Docker socket mounted a job is host root either way — so it is not what makes untrusted or fork-pull-request code safe to run. Nothing here is.
